justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assessed as the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, which I placed near 290–292. For the one-day horizon, the estimate of 291.5 essentially anchored near the current level with only a slight upward lean, reflecting the tendency of asset prices to exhibit mean-reversion or modest momentum over very short windows. At one week, I nudged the estimate to 293, acknowledging that if any near-term positive catalysts were present — such as stable macro data or supportive sentiment — prices would likely grind slightly higher rather than reverse sharply. At one month, 295 reflects a continuation of that gentle upward drift, consistent with long-run tendencies in many financial markets to drift upward at a modest pace absent significant shocks.

The width of the confidence intervals grows substantially as the horizon extends, which is the standard consequence of uncertainty compounding over time. At one day, the 90% interval of 283–300 is relatively tight because intraday and overnight price movements, while volatile, are constrained by the information already embedded in current prices. At one week, the interval widens to 275–311, capturing the possibility of meaningful news events, sentiment shifts, or technical breakouts that could move the price several percentage points in either direction. At one month, the interval of 258–332 is quite wide — roughly plus or minus 12–13% around the point estimate — reflecting how a month allows for multiple rounds of macro surprises, earnings or policy announcements, and shifts in market regime.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic conditions — such as a surprise inflation print forcing aggressive central bank action, or an unexpected geopolitical escalation — could push prices well below 258. Liquidity crises or correlated selloffs across asset classes have historically produced moves far larger than one month of normal volatility would suggest. On the upside, a strong positive surprise — such as dovish central bank guidance, better-than-expected economic data, or a relief rally following resolution of an overhang — could carry prices above 332. These tail risks are the primary reason I tried to keep the intervals honest rather than artificially narrow, though by definition a 90% interval still leaves a 10% probability of outcomes beyond either bound.
